judge_assessment.explanation: The substance is right, with one wording nuance and one omission. Problems 3 and 4 each print two required responses beyond the number: 'Which measurement did Milo actually find?' plus 'Cross out his work' (and the same for Sara), and verify.json ids 3 and 4 are single evals for 20 cm and 18 m^2. So the identification and the crossing-out are unverified and, unlike problem 8, not disclosed as manual - the judge's characterisation of them as 'explanations' is slightly loose, since the printed task is naming the measurement and marking the work rather than writing a paragraph, but both fall squarely inside the required-response-not-flagged class and the defect is real. The judge also missed a third instance of the same class: problem 6 says 'First circle the word that names what the question wants: perimeter / area', and id 6 is a single eval for 32 m, so that selection is uncovered too. Everything else checks out - all seven objective results reproduce (22 cm, 24 cm^2, 20 cm, 18 m^2, 28 m, 32 m, 9 m^2), both of problem 7's perimeters really are 20 m so the 'same fence, different space' premise is sound, and problem 8 is correctly manual with usable criteria.

strengths_to_preserve: The traps are mirrored across the pair of opening problems on identical dimensions: problem 1 (perimeter of an 8 x 3 card) declares 24 - the area - as its wrong answer, and problem 2 (area of the same card) declares 22 - the perimeter - as its wrong answer. The confusion this sheet targets is therefore diagnosable from the wrong answer alone, which is the whole point of misconception mode.

Problem 7 is well constructed: Ana's 5 x 5 square and Ben's 8 x 2 rectangle have identical 20 m perimeters but areas of 25 and 16, the stem tells the student to verify the equal-fence claim first, and the declared trap (comparing perimeters and reporting 'no difference at all', value 0) is exactly the misconception the sheet is about.

Problem 8's manual entry does the reviewer's work properly: it enumerates valid rectangle pairs for perimeter 16 (7x1 area 7, 6x2 area 12, 5x3 area 15, 4x4 area 16) rather than asserting one right answer, which is what makes an open construction gradeable by a non-specialist.

Units are declared per problem (cm, cm^2, m, m^2) and printed with the answer line, so the sheet's own rule - 'If your answer has no square in its unit, you did not find an area' - is enforced by the unit gates rather than left to the grader.

root_causes.description: SKILL.md tells the author to reframe error-analysis items 'via the ordinary types' and, a few lines later, to use manual for 'any explanation/reasoning answer'. Nothing states that an item doing both needs both entries, and no gate enforces it, so the explanation slot is dropped and the sheet reports zero manual items.
evidence: worksheet problems 3 and 4 each ask 'Which measurement did X actually find?' and 'Cross out his/her work'; verify.json ids 3 and 4 are bare evals with traps and no manual entry.
worksheet problem 6 asks the student to circle 'perimeter' or 'area'; id 6 is a bare eval for 32.
verify.json id 8 IS correctly typed manual, so the file demonstrates that the author knows the rule - what is missing is anything that forces the same treatment on the three earlier items.

root_causes.description: The coverage gate is defined per problem id, not per printed response. verify.py fails only when some id in 1..problem_count has no entry at all, so a problem that prints several required responses is fully satisfied by one scalar check, and both the gate log and the delivery message then describe the sheet as completely verified.
evidence: worksheet problem 3 prints an identification, a crossing-out and a corrected perimeter; verify.json id 3 declares one check.
worksheet problem 4 prints the same three responses; id 4 declares one check.
worksheet problem 6 prints a circled selection and a length; id 6 declares one check.

improvements.title: Require a paired manual entry for every explain / name-the-error / mark-it response
improvements.proposed_change: SKILL.md carries two rules that pull in opposite directions: the reframing paragraph says error analysis should be encoded 'via the ordinary types - the planted wrong result is checkably wrong and the correction checkably right', while the paragraph eight lines later says to use manual for 'any explanation/reasoning answer'. Authors resolve that by encoding only the numeric correction and dropping the explanation slot. Rewrite the reframing paragraph to state the pairing explicitly: an error-analysis or model-completion item that ALSO prints an explain / name-the-error / circle / cross-out / draw / label slot needs BOTH the typed check for the correction AND a manual entry for that slot under the same id (the curr-088 and curr-100 verify files in this same shard are the worked pattern). Back it with the slot gate so the rule is mechanical, not advisory. Here the pairing is needed on problems 3 and 4 (name the measurement, cross out the work) and on problem 6 (circle perimeter or area); problem 8 on the same sheet already shows the correct treatment.
improvements.regression_test: Extend tests/check_answer_slots.py with a fixture whose problem stem contains an imperative open-response verb ('Explain in one sentence', 'Circle', 'Draw', 'Label', 'Cross out', 'Which measurement did ... actually find?') and whose verify.json entry for that id is a bare eval. The gate must exit 1 demanding a paired {"type": "manual"} entry. The same fixture passes once the manual entry is added. Today it passes in both states, so the test fails before the fix.
improvements.expected_impact: The build's manual-item count becomes trustworthy: exit 2 and the 'flagged manual-review items' banner appear whenever a sheet asks a child to explain, mark or draw something, instead of the build reporting all-green on unreviewed reasoning.
improvements.risk: More sheets exit 2 rather than 0, which looks like a regression on dashboards that treat exit 0 as success. That is the intended trust signal; document it in the build-driver section of SKILL.md so exit 2 is not read as a failure.

improvements.title: Make verification coverage per printed response slot, not per problem id
improvements.proposed_change: verify.py's coverage gate currently passes as soon as every id in 1..problem_count carries one entry (scripts/verify.py, the `missing = [i for i in range(1, problem_count + 1) if i not in ids]` check). Replace that with a slot-level contract: add a build gate that counts the response slots a problem actually prints (each \ansline/\answerline/\ansblank, each \underline{} write-on rule in a stem, each lettered part (a)/(b)/(c), each row of a fill-in table or partially blank sequence) and fails the build unless that id declares at least as many verify entries. Add the matching rule to SKILL.md's JSON-format paragraph, which today only says 'every problem id 1..N has at least one check'. Problems 3, 4 and 6 each print two required responses beyond the number and declare one check each.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/check_answer_slots.py plus a fixture pair under tests/fixtures/: a worksheet .tex whose problem 1 prints two response slots (an inline \underline{} line inside the stem and \problem's automatic answer blank) and a verify.json carrying a single scalar entry for id 1. The gate must exit 1 naming 'problem 1 prints 2 response slots but declares 1 check'. Today build.sh runs that fixture green, so the test fails before the fix and passes after.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes the dominant hard-failure class in this shard: a worksheet can no longer print several required responses per problem while reporting itself fully verified.
improvements.risk: Slot counting is a heuristic over LaTeX and prose, so it will over-count on stems that use \underline for emphasis. Keep it a fail-with-named-slot gate (never a silent skip) and allow an explicit per-problem "slots" override in the verify JSON so a genuine one-slot problem can declare that rather than being blocked.

case_summary: Mathematically and pedagogically this is a strong misconception sheet: the area and perimeter formulas are correct everywhere, units are declared and gated in both directions, the first two problems mirror each other's wrong answers so the confusion is diagnosable, problem 7's equal-perimeter/different-area pair is genuinely well-chosen, and problem 8's open construction carries enumerated acceptance criteria. It is rejected for one narrow reason and I agree with it: the responses that show whether the child can TELL the two measurements apart - naming what Milo and Sara actually found, crossing out their work, and circling the word in problem 6 - are recorded among the machine-checked items with no manual disclosure, even though problem 8 on the same sheet is handled correctly. The judge's phrasing calls those responses explanations when they are identifications and markings, but the trust defect is exactly as described, and problem 6 is a third instance the verdict does not mention.
